newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Half Burundi tea exports out before sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Half Burundi tea exports out before sanctions.

text.p: About half of Burundi's annual 7,000 tonnes of tea exports were shipped before regional sanctions severed the landlocked country's trade and transport links with the outside world, a senior tea official said.

But Montfort Masunzu told Reuters about 500 tonnes of Burundi tea in 40 containers were caught at the Indian Ocean ports of Mombasa in Kenya and Dar es Salaam in Tanzania when the sanctions were imposed last July 31.
"The containers are still there and the tea is spoiling inside," said Masunzu, director of marketing at the Burundi Tea Office (OTB).
But he said in-country stocks were well-stored and would not suffer a loss in quality for several months.
The sanctions were intended as punishment for a coup on July 25 by Burundi's mainly Tutsi army and as a weapon to force new President Pierre Buyoya to talk with rebel leaders of the Hutu majority.
Masunzu told Reuters on Tuesday annual (Jan-Dec) exports -- 98 percent of tea production -- were on course for about 7,000 tonnes, or the same as last year, before the embargo.
He said 3,500 tonnes had already been shipped, excluding the 500 tonnes in stranded containers, before sanctions.

He said normal production was maintained despite the fact that tea is grown in some of the most war-torn parts of Burundi. One of OTB's five tea factories, in the dangerous and largely depopulated northwest province of Cibitoke, has been forced to close.
Burundi's small but high-quality tea crop is the country's second source of foreign currency receipts after coffee which is similarly hit by sanctions.

OTB's main problem would soon be how to pay farmers for the leaves they bring to the office's four functioning tea factories. These purchases are normally financed by export sales or by bank bridging loans, Masunzu said.
Export earnings are drying up and banks are unwilling to lend because there is no certainty the sanctions will soon be eased or lifted.
"If the state does not intervene to help, by the end of November there will be a problem paying the peasants for the leaves," he said.

The farmers have little choice but to sell to OTB since the leaves need to be brought to factory within 10 hours of picking and smuggling them across the border to Rwanda would take too long, Masunzu said.
He said Burundi's three main tea markets were Britain and Ireland followed by Pakistan and the Gulf states.
He said about 45 percent of Burundi tea was sold at London auctions, 35 percent at Mombasa auctions and the remaining 20 percent directly to buyers.
